name: clean_prose

name: rubric_case_study_full
text: I spent the morning fixing the fence. The wood had warped over winter, so two boards no longer met. My neighbour lent me a plane and we shaved them down until they sat flush.

report.note: prohibitions_clear means no hard prohibitions remain. It does NOT mean humanization is complete.
manual_review: Confirm that claims, numbers, names and stance are unchanged from the source and that the tone the user asked for is intact (AR-001). In a new draft, confirm every name, number, date, quotation and first-person experience came from the user or the source, with a marked placeholder where one is missing.

Read the draft in your head and listen for a run of sentences that march at one cadence, each the same length and shape. Look hardest at runs of short punchline fragments and one-line questions, because that is the cadence problem to find. Recombine or split those sentences by meaning until each carries one whole thought. The checker reports sentence-length numbers, and this item is the qualitative read.

The same construction restated across the piece reads as a tic even when the words differ, whether it is an antithesis ('not X, but Y'), a copula maxim or a rule of three. Vary the constructions as well as the vocabulary. A budget such as 'at most one antithesis', 'at most one appended label' or 'at most one aphorism' covers the whole piece, and checking section by section cannot enforce it, because four sections can each pass with one instance while the document holds four. Count these across every section. The checker counts some of these shapes and reports a document_budget finding, but only within the text it receives, so run the last humanizer_check_text on the assembled document as well as on the part you edited last. The shapes no detector finds are yours to count.

One contrast is ordinary writing. The tell is the reflex, the same binary reached for in section after section. The checker flags the copula frame ('It is X, not Y.') and leaves the other contrasts to you, such as "We chose depth, not breadth." and "The wordmark comes from paint on paper, not the polished apps she gave up on." A single contracted negation flip ('It's not X. It's Y.', 'This isn't a bug. It's a feature.') is also a judgment call counted across the whole piece, because the checker reports contracted flips as a document_budget finding only when the text holds two or more. The uncontracted form ('It is not a tool. It is a partner.') is flagged on its own, even once. Count every contrast and every flip across the whole piece, and rewrite the repeats as a positive claim that stands on its own.

Check whether the style shifts between sections or holds one flat fingerprint throughout. Human writers modulate, and LLMs stay even. Let each section's texture follow its job, and do not make sections differ for contrast. The checker reports cross-section uniformity, and this item is the qualitative read.

Ask whether this could have been written about almost any topic, by almost anyone. Cut smooth but empty phrasing, reflexive hedges and motivational closers. State the point of view the user or the source holds, and keep the concrete, specific, checkable details the source or the user gives, never invented (see AR-001).

An abstract noun ('the gap', 'the work', 'the craft', 'the order') used as the subject of an agentive or experiential verb (mattered, decided, kept, taught, carries, carried, holds, demands) reads fluently while no one in the sentence does anything. Metaphorical 'carry' is the most frequent instance and the hardest to hear ('the layout carries the weight', 'the silence carried the room', 'eight words to carry'), because the verb performs gravity while the sentence names no actor and no effect. Prefer a human or concrete subject, and say what the thing does. The checker catches the fixed collocations, and the open-ended cases are yours to read for. Time and calendar nouns count too, and they are the hardest to hear because they read as a lively figure ('the Fridays survived', 'Busy season eats the Fridays', 'Billiards survives final year', 'Work does not get to claim them'). Read for a schedule, a job or an activity that 'decides', 'wins' or 'gives back'. Name the person and say what happens ('I still make it to billiards on Fridays'). Ideas and artifacts slip in the same way, most often inside a maxim about the work ('the answer usually costs you the design you arrived with', 'A design that ignores the build comes back', 'the only thing I do that asks me to stand still'). None of these has a word the checker could anchor on.

A performative framing beat is a sentence or label whose job is to perform insight, closure or self-awareness instead of carrying content. It takes three forms. (a) A self-satisfied closer is a neat aphorism ending a section that adds no new fact, name or number, often crediting the author or pivoting on a tidy antithesis ('The data set is public; the reading of it is mine.'). (b) First-person meta-commentary on the work itself ('my take', 'the reading of it is mine', 'as I see it') turns up in a piece meant to be evidence-led. (c) A clever paradox headline is used to sound sharp where a plain statement of the point would do. Delete the beat and end on the last substantive point. Keep at most one aphoristic or paradox construction per piece, and only where it does analytical work. The device is human in moderation, and the tell is repetition and substitution for content. A standalone meta-label ('in 200 words', 'in brief') is the same beat. Short cells and captions have their own versions, such as the clipped verdict that performs a decision ('Tutoring stays.'), the stance closer that points back at a number already given ('and I want to keep it there') and the tidy aphoristic closer that rounds off a plain list ('four months is a long time to wait', 'tires me out more than any lecture did'). Replace each with the next concrete fact. Captions have a numeric version, the verbless pair that sets one against many ('One count, four moments', 'Three sizes, all the same height.', 'One app, every chat.'). Ordinary terse writing uses the same shape ('Two adults, one child.', 'Two tablets, every four hours.', 'Three goals, one assist.'), so judge each pair by whether it reports a fact or performs one. A maxim that hands the verdict to a third party is the same beat ('and the developer is right to send it back').

Check whether every point lines up too neatly, with each example fitting perfectly, every thread resolved and no loose ends or tension left. Human writing has friction, such as a caveat that complicates the thesis, a digression, an example that only mostly fits or a point left partly open. A frictionless argument is itself a tell. Keep the friction the source has (a caveat, an exception, a point left open) instead of smoothing it away, and add none it lacks (AR-001).

An appended significance label is a heading, subtitle or dek that names its subject and then annexes a second element promising the subject matters. It can be a reduced relative ('Reintegration support at the moment of release, and the officer the whole system turns on.'), an appositive that asserts a hinge, or a WH clause pre-defending a choice ('Method, and why this one'). Read every label in the piece and ask whether the part after the comma adds a fact or only tells the reader this is important. Cut it and let the section earn it. One such label may be deliberate. Two or more in one piece is the tell, because a repeated rhetorical shape is what reads as machine-made. The budget is one per document, counted across the assembled whole, because each check sees only the text it is given. The checker catches the WH form, and the reduced-relative and appositive forms are yours to read for, as in 'The rebuild, and the one decision that made it possible.' and 'Nine months of rework, and the meeting that started it.'

Run this pass (the Orwell pass) after the fix rounds and before the final rubric="full" check on the assembled document, and read the draft once more for three marks of flabby prose that the other layers miss. (a) Look for stale figures of speech, meaning any image you did not choose deliberately ('moves the needle', 'the federal purse', 'the tip of the iceberg'). The checker knows a closed list, and the class is open, so read for it. Replace the figure with the number or the name it stood in for and leave out any fresher figure. (b) Cut every word that can go. This rule does the most work in anything longer than a page, and the padding phrases in lexical_patterns.orwell.padding_phrases are a starting point for it. (c) Use the active where it will do and name who did it, keeping the passive in method and regulatory writing where it is the norm. One carve-out always applies. A domain term with no everyday equivalent (statutory release, Protected B, an API, a subpoena) is defined in plain words at first use and then used plainly. Do not swap it for a vaguer everyday word, because that loses the meaning the argument runs on. Then run humanizer_check_text on the trimmed text and confirm prohibitions_clear is true, because cutting words can create or expose findings such as a comma splice or a new run-on.

Section-to-section variation is among the most durable human signals, and word swaps alone leave the draft's shape as it was. Look past vocabulary to the constructions and to how each section reads, and keep the plain word where it is the right one.

Anaphora means three or more consecutive sentences opening on the same word or the same two words ('They assume users will pay. They assume the market is ready. They assume nothing changes.'). Read the run and decide whether the repetition does work or fills space. The form itself is legitimate and has a name. Thoreau wrote 'It does not keep the country free. It does not settle the West. It does not educate.', and Melville 'Forty years of continual whaling! Forty years of privation, and peril, and storm-time!' (deliberate anaphora that builds). The tell is the same construction used without escalation, where each limb restates the first instead of advancing it, and where cutting the repetition would cost the passage nothing. The figure and the tell share one syntax, so the checker cannot separate them and this one is yours to judge. The checker catches only a run that opens on This, These or the pronoun it. Allow at most one deliberate anaphoric run per document, counted across the assembled whole, and make it the strongest passage in the piece. If it is not, cut it.

Check whether a sentence explains what the image, line or example before it already showed ('He slammed the door. He was angry.'). Professional writers often cut this kind of sentence from LLM drafts, and newer models still write it. Cut the explanation and trust the reader.

This applies to essays, blog posts, opinion pieces and cover letters, and leaves reference and technical copy alone. Check whether the piece holds a single I, you or question to the reader. LLM essays use markedly less interactional language (stance, engagement and questions to the reader) than human ones. Add one only where it carries a position the user or the source holds, and never as decoration.

Readers recognise a set of defaults. Quote attributions rotate through 'notes', 'explains' and 'emphasizes' where a reporter would write 'says' every time. Every bullet opens with a bold label and a colon. Emoji sit at the start of headings or bullets. Characters get stock names ('Emily', 'Sarah', 'Dr. Chen', 'Elara'). Expert annotators cite each of these. Use the plain form unless the house style asks for the other one.

A cause-to-benefit 'so' tail is a sentence that states a mechanism and then appends ', so' plus the payoff it promises the reader ('Quip updates itself, so a fix reached people within a day of shipping.', 'Only the width changes, so the window stays under the menu-bar icon and nothing jumps away from the pointer.'). It reads as a product brochure explaining its own value. The shape is too common in plain prose for the checker, so read for it. Keep the 'so' when the reader needs the causal link, and cut it when the second half only tells them the first half was good. Often the fix is to keep one half, either the fact or the user's experience of it.

Watch for lines that tell the writer's history as a tidy sequence or describe their own habits approvingly, such as 'Ten years of teaching neurodivergent and multilingual learners came first, and so did the habit of watching where people get stuck.', 'Before them came two web tools for English learners.', 'The job was watching someone try to make sense of something complicated...', 'I design the screens, build them in code, and keep the Figma files behind them tidy.' and 'People I've never met use it'. Each sounds like a voice performing modesty or craft. State the fact with its date or number ('Teaching neurodivergent and multilingual learners since 2016.') and drop the adjective about yourself. The shape 'X came first, and so did the habit of Y' is yours to read for, because 'Prices rose, and so did the practice of haggling.' is the same construction in ordinary prose.

Ask whether someone who has never used the product could follow each sentence of product, portfolio or case-study copy on first read. Three failures recur. (a) Mechanism is written as a chain of clauses instead of saying what the user gets ('Show them in every space and they stay at the top of the sidebar, with one sign-in and one unread count, while the rest of the list changes.'). (b) The copy uses the product's own internal words, or verbs users never say ('cut across all of them', 'Filing a GIF' (nobody files GIFs), 'nothing of the app is drawn inside Chorus'). (c) A slogan has a second half that is clever and impossible to picture ('Every chat and inbox in one Mac window, and only what's new turns red.'). Also cut vague casual counts ('a dozen or so testers'), run-in labels ('The worst bug:') and release-by-release history ('first release 13 July'). Write short sentences in plain words, use a UX term where it is the right term, and define any product concept before using it.

Then run one last check on the assembled document with rubric="full" and do the self-review against your draft, changing only the spans an item points to. If the self-review changed anything, run humanizer_check_text once more and confirm prohibitions_clear is true before returning.

name: ai/ai_cover_letter_01.txt
text:
Over the past five years I have taught first-year composition, advanced argumentation, and a sophomore seminar in rhetorical theory, designing each syllabus around the conviction that students write best when they have something real at stake in the page. My composition sections move students from personal narrative toward research-driven argument over the term, and I have found that the bridge between those modes is where the most durable learning happens. I treat revision not as cleanup but as rethinking, and I structure my courses so that no major essay is submitted without at least one full round of substantive rewriting.

Alongside the classroom, I spent three years staffing our university writing center, where I worked one-on-one with students from every discipline. Those tutoring hours taught me to diagnose a draft quickly and to ask the question that helps a writer find their own way forward.

name: ai/ai_cover_letter_02.txt
text:
For the past three years I have coordinated communications for a youth mentorship program serving roughly two hundred families across the county. I wrote the monthly newsletter, managed our presence on Instagram and Facebook, and built the email campaigns that pushed our spring enrollment up by nearly a third. Working with young people taught me to write the way our families actually talk, warm and direct, never talking down to anyone, and I believe that voice is exactly what an education nonprofit needs in its public messaging.

What draws me to this role specifically is the chance to do that work at a larger scale and for a mission I already care about. I have managed a content calendar across multiple platforms, tracked engagement to learn what genuinely resonated, and turned a modest budget into steady audience growth. I would be glad to bring that same hands-on approach to your team.

name: ai/ai_cover_letter_03.txt
text:
For four years I worked as a case aide at a community center serving children who had been referred to us by schools, social workers, and the courts. Many of them arrived guarded, having learned that adults don't always stick around, and a good part of my job was simply proving otherwise week after week. I ran our after-school homework club, coordinated transportation for kids whose families couldn't manage the pickup, and sat in on the case reviews where our staff decided how best to support each child.

That experience taught me that coordinating a program for vulnerable children is as much about logistics as it is about heart. Schedules slip, funding shifts, and a single missed handoff can mean a child falls through the cracks. I learned to keep the moving pieces organized without ever losing sight of the kids at the center of them, and I would bring that same steadiness to the coordinator role you've posted.

name: ai/ai_cover_letter_04.txt
text:
I believe a classroom works best when children feel safe enough to be wrong out loud. In my four years teaching third and fourth grade, I have built my practice around that idea, designing lessons that invite kids to guess, test, and revise rather than wait nervously for the one right answer. When a student feels free to take a risk, the learning takes care of itself.

In practice, that means a lot of hands-on work and a lot of talking through problems together. I use small reading groups so I can meet each child where they actually are, and I lean on math manipulatives so that abstract ideas have something concrete to stand on. I also keep families in the loop, because the children who thrive are usually the ones whose parents and teacher are pulling in the same direction. I would be honored to bring that approach to your school.

name: ai/ai_marketing_01.txt
text:
Most earbuds give you one fit and expect your ears to cooperate. Ours don't. Each pair ships with a range of tips and a guided fit test that finds the exact seal your ears were waiting for, so they stay put through a run, a commute, or a long flight without that constant nudge-them-back-in routine.

That perfect seal does more than keep them in place. It's what lets the active noise cancellation do its job, sealing out the rumble of an airplane cabin or the hum of an open office so the only thing left is your music. Switch to transparency mode with a tap when you need to hear the world again. Eight hours on a single charge, with three more in the case. Built for people who'd rather not think about their earbuds at all.

name: ai/ai_marketing_02.txt
text:
Pack it, drop it, drag it through a downpour, and it shrugs the whole thing off. This 60-liter duffel is cut from heavyweight coated fabric with welded, weather-sealed seams, so a sudden storm on the tarmac or a wet boat deck won't reach the gear inside. The base is reinforced where bags take the most abuse, and the zippers are the chunky, gloved-hand kind that won't jam when you're cold and in a hurry.

Sixty liters swallows a week of clothes and still has room for boots. Padded backpack straps tuck away when you'd rather carry it by the grab handles, and a separate ventilated end pocket keeps muddy or damp items away from everything else. Whether it's riding in a truck bed or checked under a plane, this is the bag you stop worrying about.

At 35 liters, this carry-on hits the sweet spot: big enough for a long weekend or a fast-and-light week, small enough to stay with you through the cabin door and into the overhead bin. No checked bag, no waiting at the carousel, no lost luggage.

A padded laptop sleeve and a clamshell opening let you pack and find things like a suitcase rather than digging to the bottom. Load-bearing hip and chest straps shift the weight off your shoulders on long walks between gates or trailheads. Toss it in an overhead, strap it to your back, and just go.

text:
There's a reason wool has kept people warm for a few thousand years, and this vest is a quiet argument for sticking with what works. It's knit from a dense, springy wool that traps heat without the bulk, so you get the warmth of a thick layer in something you can wear under a shell or on its own. The fibers breathe as you move, wicking moisture and shedding the clammy overheated feeling that sinks synthetic layers.

Cut for real movement, with armholes that don't bind when you reach. The natural crimp of the wool helps it resist odor and bounce back into shape after a long day. This is the layer you'll reach for on cold mornings and keep reaching for, year after year.

name: ai/ai_prose_01.txt
text:
When I was small, the line between work and play seemed obvious. Play was anything I'd have done on my own. Work was the stuff grown-ups invented to ruin a perfectly good afternoon: rake the leaves, set the table, finish the math sheet before the cartoons. Nobody had to teach me the difference. I felt it in my gut, the way you feel the difference between a hill you're running down and one you're trudging up.

So I grew up assuming a job was just chores with a paycheck stapled to them. Something done because somebody made you, not because you wanted to. It took me an embarrassingly long time to notice the cracks in that idea, to meet adults who chased their work the way I once chased fireflies. I'm still unlearning it. Some mornings the old kid-logic creeps back in, and the alarm clock sounds exactly like my mother calling me inside.

name: ai/ai_prose_02.txt
text:
My brother lives four time zones away now. I see him at Christmas, maybe once in the summer if the flights line up. Add it up and we're talking eight, ten days a year. We're both in our thirties. Be generous and say we each get another forty years. That's four hundred days. Less than a year and a half of his company, total, spread across the rest of my life.

I did this math one night and couldn't shake it. The people I assumed were permanent fixtures turn out to be on a countdown I never noticed starting. Friends scatter, parents age, everyone has their own gravity now. I'm not telling you this to be morbid. I'm telling you because I booked a flight the next morning.

name: ai/ai_prose_03.txt
text:
Ask anyone how they're doing lately and you'll get the same answer. Busy. So busy. Slammed, swamped, underwater. We say it with a sigh, but listen closely and there's something else underneath, a little flicker of pride dressed up as exhaustion.

Being busy has quietly become the thing we brag about. Nobody wants to admit they had a slow week, that they read a novel on the couch and went to bed early. That sounds like failure now, like you're not in demand. So we inflate our calendars and complain about them in the same breath, and everyone nods along because they're doing it too.

I caught myself doing it last week. Someone asked how I was, and before I'd even thought about it, out came the word. Busy. I wasn't, particularly. I just didn't know how else to sound like I mattered.

name: ai/ai_prose_04.txt
text:
I found a shoebox of my old drawings last month, tucked behind the winter coats. Hundreds of them. Spaceships, mostly, and maps of countries that never existed, drawn on the backs of my dad's office printouts. I must have been nine or ten. I'd forgotten I ever did this, and there it was in front of me, proof that I once spent whole weekends inventing worlds and didn't think it strange at all.

Somewhere around thirteen I just stopped. Not a dramatic quitting, no decision I can point to. The pencils went into a drawer and the drawer got buried under other things, the way everything does at that age. I think I decided drawing was something little kids did, and I had bigger ideas about who I was becoming.

What gets me is that nobody made me stop. I gave it up all on my own, for reasons I can't even reconstruct now. So last week I bought a sketchbook. The first pages are terrible. I don't care even a little.

name: ai/ai_technical_01.txt
text:
Git can feel intimidating before you've actually used it, but the core idea is simple: it keeps a complete history of your project so you can experiment freely and never lose work. In this tutorial, you'll learn the two ways every project begins. The first is starting fresh, where you take a folder on your own machine and turn it into a Git repository with a single command. The second is cloning, where you grab a copy of a project that already exists somewhere else, usually a service like GitHub, and bring the whole thing down to your computer with its full history intact.

Knowing which one you need is half the battle, and beginners mix them up all the time. By the end, you'll be comfortable telling the two apart, and you'll have done both yourself. You'll create a brand-new repository from scratch, clone an existing one, and understand what's actually happening on disk in each case. No prior Git experience required, just a terminal and a few minutes.

name: ai/ai_technical_02.txt
text:
When you install a package in Python, it has to go somewhere, and by default it lands in a single shared location tied to your system's Python. That works fine until you're juggling two projects that need different versions of the same library. Suddenly one project breaks every time you set up the other, and you're left wondering what changed.

Virtual environments solve this. A virtual environment is an isolated folder with its own copy of Python and its own private set of installed packages, walled off from everything else. In this tutorial, we'll look at how Python actually finds and loads the packages you import, why the default shared setup causes trouble, and how giving each project its own environment makes the whole problem disappear.

name: ai/ai_technical_03.txt
text:
If you've spent any time administering a Linux system, you've run into systemd, whether you wanted to or not. It's the first thing that starts when the machine boots, and it's responsible for bringing nearly everything else to life. At the heart of it sits a single concept: the unit.

A unit is just systemd's name for something it knows how to manage. That might be a background service, a mounted filesystem, a network socket, or a scheduled timer. Each one is described by a plain-text configuration file called a unit file, and once you can read and write those, systemd stops feeling like magic. This guide walks through what units are, the common types you'll meet, and how to write a unit file of your own.

name: ai/ai_technical_04.txt
text:
JavaScript is the programming language of the web browser. If a web page does anything beyond just sitting there, chances are JavaScript is behind it. When you click a button and a menu slides open, when a form warns you about a missing field before you hit submit, when new posts load as you scroll without the page reloading, that's JavaScript at work.

It helps to see where it fits. A web page is built from three technologies that each do a different job. HTML provides the structure, the headings and paragraphs and buttons. CSS handles how everything looks, the colors, fonts, and layout. JavaScript adds the behavior, the part that responds to what you do. In this article we'll unpack what JavaScript actually is, what it lets you build, and why it became the language that makes the web interactive.
